title: The Dutch Water Boards
text:
Much of the western Netherlands lies at or below sea level. From the Middle Ages, as people drained peat bogs and marshes to farm them, the land sank, and the sea and rivers constantly threatened to flood it. No single farmer could hold back the water alone. A dike is only as strong as its weakest stretch, and a breach on one man's land drowns his neighbors too.

So communities organized. Landowners in each area were made responsible for maintaining sections of dikes and ditches, and inspectors walked the dikes to check that each had done his part. Over the thirteenth century these local arrangements grew into regional water boards, the waterschappen, with their own officials, led by a dike reeve. The Hoogheemraadschap van Rijnland, one of the oldest, traces its origins to the middle of the thirteenth century.

The boards worked on a simple principle often summarized as interest, payment, say: those who benefited from protection paid for it, and in return had a voice in how the board was run. They could levy taxes, make rules and punish people who neglected their dikes. Their authority rested on the shared danger, which everyone understood.

Water boards still exist in the Netherlands, now fewer and larger, and their members are still elected by local residents. They are among the oldest democratic institutions in the country, and many Dutch people trace their habit of consultation and compromise, sometimes called the polder model, to the long need to manage water together.
lesson: A common threat can teach neighbors to govern together. When everyone depends on everyone else's part, shared rules and a shared say keep the team strong.
people: Dutch landowners, dike reeves and water board members
source: Water board charters; William H. TeBrake, Medieval Frontier: Culture and Ecology in Rijnland (1985)
caveat: The link between medieval water boards and modern Dutch consensus politics is a popular interpretation rather than an established fact.
